title: I’m a solo dev running 8 Claude Code agents as a “team” to build a cozy browser MMO. Here’s the workflow, what it gets right, and where it breaks
author: DisastrousJacket4738
selftext:
I’m building TinyHQ, a cozy pixel town you play in the browser: you build a homestead, adopt a pet, keep hens, and hang out with whoever’s around. It’s free to play, with optional Watts packs. I’m one person. Most of the code, the reviews, and a lot of the art pipeline come from a set of Claude Code sessions I run like a small studio. I wanted to share how that’s set up, because the setup has mattered more than the prompts.

**The setup**

* **Eight “seats”, each a long-running Claude Code session with a lane:**
   * world (places and the room server);
   * economy (shop, payments, Watts);
   * art (furniture and the sprite pipeline);
   * scene (rendering and the golf minigame);
   * two front-end seats;
   * a performance/QA seat;
   * a “feedback” seat that plays the live site like a new player and reports what’s broken or confusing.
* **Each seat gets its own git worktree and branch.** It works an issue from Linear and writes a READY note when it’s done: what changed, what it tested, shots.
* **A separate “manager” session never writes features.** It hands out jobs and answers questions. Every READY goes to a fresh, read-only reviewer agent that only reads the diff. That agent can’t check out, test or deploy. It writes Musts and Shoulds, and nothing merges with an open Must.
* **Approved branches go to a merge agent in batches.** It runs the gates: typecheck, about 10,000 tests in shards, a hard cap on the main bundle size, a database security check, a 42-step smoke test against the live site, then the deploy. Today it shipped four batches.
* **I’m the only human.** I play the builds, make the design calls, and hold the money, the secrets and the feature switches. Agents never touch payment settings or flip a live switch without my say-so.
* **The game itself makes no AI calls at runtime.** The AI is in how it’s built, not in what you play.

**What actually works**

* **Separate reviewer agents catch real bugs.** One branch today let a malformed database password crash the servers on startup. The crash message could also print the password into the logs. The reviewer caught it, and the author agent fixed it in about 20 minutes. Another review caught a golf feature doing server work while golf was switched off.
* **Small branches in narrow lanes.** Most of my merge pain came from two agents editing the same file. Lanes and per-seat worktrees cut that down a lot.
* **Written rules beat repeated prompting.** House rules live in files every session reads: our player-facing words (“homestead”, never “office”), no paid randomness, permissive licences only, migration numbering. A fresh session follows them better than any long prompt I’ve written.
* **The “feedback” seat** plays the live site at phone and desktop sizes and reports wording slips, broken steps and stale copy. It’s the most useful thing I added this month.

**What breaks**

* **Coordination is the real cost.** Today two seats picked the same database migration number. Now the manager hands out numbers from a queue file.
* **Context runs out.** Long sessions fill up and need compacting, and sometimes they lose the thread mid-task. Short jobs with written briefs help.
* **The machine is the bottleneck.** Eight agents plus headless browsers pinned my PC at 100% CPU. That made our own uptime monitor report outages that never happened: the monitor itself was too starved to read the answers in time. One agent traced it back by matching the failed checks against the PC’s crash logs.
* **Agents are confidently wrong about the product.** Prose about the game drifts from what’s actually live. Every post and store page now gets an agent fact-check against the code before it goes out. Today’s caught six overclaims.
* **Taste is still mine.** Agents can build a gate that animates. They can’t tell you it should feel like walking through a garden gate rather than a locked door. That came from me playing it.

**Questions for you**

* If you run more than one agent: how do you split the work? By feature, by layer, or by file ownership?
* Has anyone found a good way to give agents a sense of how a game *feels*, beyond screenshots and written notes?
* How do you handle reviews: same model, different model, or a human pass on everything?

Happy to go deeper on any part of it: the review prompts, the merge gates, the art pipeline.

The game, if you want to see the result (free, in the browser, 18+): [https://revpain.itch.io/tinyhq](https://revpain.itch.io/tinyhq)
